About 1 min

Operationalizing CRSP in High School Biology

For: teachers who believe in culturally responsive-sustaining pedagogy (CRSP) and want to know what it looks like on an average class day. It’s especially for science teachers who suspect their content is “culturally neutral.”

Guiding Questions:

  • What does it mean to operationalize culturally responsive teaching?
  • How do we keep Culturally Responsive Teaching from becoming a buzzword, and center it as a pedagogical approach that disrupts inequitable practices?

Sources: my student-teaching placement, a mixed 9th/10th-grade Biology class with Honors and Standard students in the same room. The school is a public mid-sized arts magnet high school, and its students are highly economically disadvantaged.

Argument: In this classroom, care is built into the foundations. Every student has a one-on-one conference each quarter, and the teacher checks in with every student every day. The academic push of the warm demander is optional: on a recent review assignment, the hardest thinking was extra credit for Standard students, and none of them attempted it. Operationalizing CRSP means making the push as structural as the care.

Consider for a moment: Think of one routine in your classroom that every student experiences. Is it a routine of care, of push, or both?

What it means to operationalize CRSP

About 2 min

My definition

Culturally responsive teaching is a pedagogical framework in which the teacher builds trusting relationships with students and designs classes, lessons, and strategies that start from what students already know and how they learn, pushes all students toward academic success, and gives students the academic tools to challenge inequity, recognize ideology, and question ideas that promote the status quo. Culturally sustaining pedagogy adds an emphasis on intentionally recognizing, encouraging, and promoting cultural pluralism in schools.

From belief to practice

Zaretta Hammond clearly identifies the primary challenge: teachers struggle to turn culturally responsive principles into practices. She defines culturally responsive teaching as recognizing how students display learning and make meaning. The teacher then uses that cultural knowledge as a scaffold to new content, in the context of a relationship that makes the classroom feel safe (Hammond, 2015). Operationalizing is moving from belief to practice.

Belief Practice at my placement
Trust comes before rigor. Every student has a one-on-one conference each quarter that opens with strengths
Every student deserves to be seen and spoken to every day. The teacher circulates a fixed path during every lesson and checks in with each student by name.
Student knowledge is valuable. In the cell metaphor project, students invent their own analogy for the cell, in their preferred language.
All students deserve higher-order work. Not yet a practice. The hardest questions are extra credit for Standard students.

A three-question buzzword test for teacher practices:

  1. Does it change what how students process content, or only how the room looks and sounds? Surface cultural references don’t build students’ capacity to think (Hammond, 2015).
  2. Does it reach every student, or only those who opt in? Optional, extra-credit work tends to widen the gaps its was intended to close (Feldman, 2024).
  3. Does it treat what students bring as assets or as deficits to fix? Deficit thinking assumes students and families lack what school values (Hammond, 2015).

Ready for Rigor at my placement

About 3 min

Hammond’s Ready for Rigor framework has four practice areas that only work together: Awareness, Learning Partnerships, Information Processing, and Community of Learners (Hammond, 2015).

I will examine two of them in detail. My rating scale: not yet, partly, consistently.

Learning Partnerships: Consistent Care, Questionable Push

Hammond describes a learning partnership as rapport plus alliance, which together produce cognitive insight into how a student learns (Hammond, 2015).

Element What I saw Rating
Rapport Each quarterly conference opens with how the student is doing and what they think they do well. Students often reveal things the teacher didn’t know: home situations, seating needs, organizational struggles, a wish to drop to Standard. This exemplifies Hammond’s “pedagogy of listening” (Hammond, 2015). Consistently
Alliance Each student sets a goal and picks an action step, and the teacher asks, “How can I help you achieve this goal?” The list of possible action steps is almost all behavior and organization oriented (tutoring, binder, missing work, bedtime alarms). Goals are framed around the grade, and the next check-in is a quarter (two months) away. Hammond’s idea of a learning “pact” instead targets a small, specific, significant learning goal, with more frequent benchmarks (Hammond, 2015). Partly
Care and push Hammond’s warm demander model pairs personal warmth with active demand for academic effort. Warmth without demand leans toward the “sentimentalist,” who protects students from struggle (Hammond, 2015). In this class the warmth is structural. However, the highest-level thinking is optional for Standard students, and none attempted it on the photosynthesis review assignment. Partly

Information Processing: Uneven access to rigor

This practice area asks teachers to provide real challenge, connect content to students’ lives, and teach cognitive routines (Hammond, 2015).

Element What I saw How fully
Processing through metaphor In the cell metaphor project, students invent their own analogy for the whole cell and justify each organelle’s role. This is an example of the similarities-and-differences and whole-to-part routines (Hammond, 2015). It draws on students’ pre-existing funds of knowledge, making it easier for them to connect to content and more likely to retain it. Yet the rubric gives 13 of its 50 points to logistics and looks (on time, title, names, color) and only 12 to whether the metaphors make sense, which calls into question what the point of the grade is. Partly
Appropriate challenge for all students The photosynthesis review assignment moves up in Bloom’s verbs from recall to reasoning. The experimental-design skills (variables, constants, means, graph validity) are required for Honors but extra credit for Standard. Hammond warns that underserved students routinely get less higher-order work, with challenge postponed until “the basics” are mastered (Hammond, 2015). Not yet
Connecting to students’ lives Units rarely connect to students’ communities. Hammond argues science actually can: through oral-tradition processing strategies and problem-based units based in students’ lived experiences (Hammond, 2015). Not yet

My observation: An advanced physics class at the same school offers a contrast to the “cookbook” predetermined-outcome labs we perform: there, small groups designed their own lab procedures. See Part 2, Artifact 3.

Consider for a moment: In your class, what opportunities are available to everyone, and which are offered only to students that are already labeled as being advanced?

HLP spotlight on building respectful relationships

About 2 min

What the practice is. Teachers intentionally build relationships marked by trust, care and appreciation of students’ cultures and communities. They manage power so that more students participate. The practice breaks down into four key areas: establishing rapport, building mutual trust, monitoring and maintaining relationships, and examining oneself (TeachingWorks, 2026).

Relationships are the foundation of learning!

Where I see it in my internship placement:

  • Daily contact routine. The teacher walks a fixed circulation path and checks in with every student by name (Artifact 4). Students wave the teacher over, often more than once a period. They answer honestly about how their work is going, make small talk, and ask unusual and personal questions (which don’t necessary get answered, but demonstrate rapport). This daily contact catches the quiet, middle-of-the-pack students who are good at “playing school” and rarely hear from teachers.
  • Scheduled conferences. Each student has a quarterly one-on-one conference (Artifact 1). It ends with the question, “Are there things you would like to see change in Biology?”, which gives students some control over their learning. The teacher makes it clear that they are a learning partner who is listening to the student.
  • In a different classroom. Another Biology teacher at my school kept a conversational rapport while stating expectations clearly. When a student asked to make a phone call, the teacher restated the rule briefly and moved on.

How these practices could be strengthened

  1. Collect data. For two weeks, tally positive, neutral and negative interactions with 3–5 focal students. Hammond suggests at least two positive interactions for every neutral or negative one (Hammond, 2015).
  2. Check your classroom map. Does your walking path prioritize interactions with some tables more than others?
  3. Learning pacts. During student conferences, add one skill target, such as writing a complete CER, and conduct a mid-quarter check-in related directly to that goal several weeks later.

Community cultural wealth

About 2 min

Yosso names at least six forms of capital that communities of color build and use to survive and resist oppression (Yosso, 2005). Here are four, each with a classroom practice I have observed at my internship placement that draws on it and one that overlooks it.

Form Definition Draws on it Overlooks it Possible Improvement
Aspirational Keeping hopes and dreams alive despite real and perceived barriers (Yosso, 2005) Students graph every assessment on a progress tracker, set goals, plan and celebrate trends. Trackers and conference goals center scores and grades, so learning (and hope) can be reduced to desperate grabs for points. This is the “commodity of grades” (Feldman, 2024). Add a skills column to the progress tracker, to broaden the scope of what is being tracked beyond simply grades.
Linguistic Skills from communicating in more than one language or style, including storytelling, art, music and poetry (Yosso, 2005) The cell metaphor project can be done in a student’s preferred language; four of 50 students did, three in Spanish and one in Mandarin Chinese. Daily notes and assignments are English-only. Tests can be switched to another language digitally, but only for students who know to ask. Bilingual key-term glossaries, and same language choice on classwork.
Familial Knowledge developed via family, including models of caring and coping (Yosso, 2005) After each conference, students email their family, and families almost always reply with appreciation. The email informs families but doesn’t ask them anything. Add a question for the family, e.g. what their student does well at home.
Navigational Skills for moving through institutions not built with communities of color in mind (Yosso, 2005) Conferences bring students’ wishes to change class (honors/standard) to the surface, so the teacher can help them navigate. Moving up depends on teacher advocacy and on optional extra credit that Standard students generally don’t attempt. Extra credit favors students with more resources (Feldman, 2024). Require the higher-order questions of everyone, and use them as evidence for class placement.

Consider for a moment: Pick one student you know well. Which form of capital do they bring that your class never asks them to use?

Where it’s not yet happening, and my next steps

About 1 min

CRSP is not yet fully operationalized at my placement. Here are four specific gaps.

Gap Evidence Concrete change
Higher-order thinking is optional for Standard students. On the photosynthesis review, experimental-design questions were extra credit for Standard students, and none attempted them. Require them of everyone, with scaffolds. If the work is important, require it (Feldman, 2024).
Grades value appearance and timing over thinking. On the cell metaphor rubric, 13 of 50 points go to logistics and looks, while only 12 go to whether the metaphors make sense. Re-weight rubrics toward reasoning, and grade lateness separately from learning (Feldman, 2024).
Daily materials are English-only. Notes and assignments have no translations. Translated tests are available only on request. Bilingual key-term glossaries, and a language choice on classwork.
Biology is taught as culturally neutral. Units rarely touch students’ communities or the history of who did science we are learning about in class today. In the cell unit, add Henrietta Lacks and HeLa cells (consent and racism in medicine).

My next steps

Named action How I’ll know it’s working
First year teacher Replace one semester exam with a student-choice final project: students choose the medium, format and content. One shared rubric for every format, and the work is done in class. Survey students on whether they were able to show what they know.
Long term Redesign one unit per year around a real-world anchoring phenomenon, co-planned with a colleague and shaped by a student interest survey. A unit-end survey on whether the unit was relevant to students’ lives.

Consider for a moment: Which of these four gaps exists in your own classroom? Which change could you make before your next unit?

Evidence

About 6 min

Five artifacts from two settings: my placement Biology classroom, and an advanced physics classroom at the same school.

Each piece of evidence will follow the describe, interpret, evaluate protocol (Hammond, 2015).

Artifact 1: Quarterly one-on-one conference

Context and resources: Student prep sheet and teacher conference plan · Placement Biology class · Before the end of each quarter.

What is happening. Before their conference, students fill out an exit ticket. They name two things they’ve done well, looking beyond the grade to labs, participation and growth from CDA to test. They write their current grade, set a goal for the quarter, and check at least one action step. In the conference, the teacher asks about strengths and the student’s self-assigned goal, then asks, “How can I help you achieve this goal?” The teacher then adds a goal of their own for the student and invites questions and “things you would like to see change in Biology.” The student then emails their family from a template, copying the teacher. Students respond very positively to these conferences and often reveal things the teacher didn’t know: home situations, seating needs, organizational struggles, a wish to change level. Families almost always reply with appreciation.

What it shows. This is an example of the alliance building that is necessary for forming a learning partnership (Hammond, 2015). It helps the teacher build respectful relationships and draws on aspirational and familial capital (Yosso, 2005).

What’s missing. The action steps are almost all behavioral, and often assume home resources (“create a quiet space at home”). Goals generally focus on the grade, the family email is one-way by default, and there is no system to check in regarding a goal mid-quarter before the next conference.

Artifact 2: Photosynthesis review with “Honors only” questions

Context and resources: Review assignment · Placement Biology class · Photosynthesis unit

What is happening. Questions 1–10 are recall with word banks and diagram labels. Questions 11–21, marked “Everyone completes,” ask students to reason from a plant-bubble experiment: identify the control, make a claim about light and rate, estimate and explain. Questions 22–23 are “required for Honors, but extra credit for Standard”: judge a graph’s validity, identify variables and constants, choose a data display, calculate means and draw a conclusion. No Standard student attempted them.

What it shows. Everyone gets an opportunity to show scientific reasoning, which is a strength of the assignment. Other importance scientific skills are restricted according to a student’s class: Standard students tend to get less higher-order work. This aligns with Hammond’s ideas about struggling students often having challenges postponed until “the basics” are mastered (Hammond, 2015). Optional extra credit tends to be taken advantage of by students with more resources (Feldman, 2024). Because moving up to Honors depends on demonstrating mastery of this kind of extra work, the course design also leans on navigational capital in a negative way (Yosso, 2005).

What should change. Make questions 22–23 required for everyone, with scaffolds such as a worked example and sentence frames.

Artifact 3: Student-designed lab in an advanced physics class

Context and resources: Observation notes · Advanced physics classroom at the same school

No physical artifact: this evidence comes from my written observation notes.

What is happening. Small groups investigated motion. Each group developed its own procedure and collected its own data. The teacher stayed available, asked eliciting questions about procedures and data, and pointed students back to lab materials when they got stuck. Students collaborated productively and used technology responsibly.

What it shows. These students acted like Hammond’s portrait of an independent learner: they attempted new tasks without scaffolds and had strategies for getting unstuck (Hammond, 2015). This is small-group work that requires collaboration. Unlike a lab with prescribed steps and a known outcome (a “cookbook” lab), the investigation requires students to decide how to collect useful evidence and how to evaluate it (Windschitl et al., 2018).

Relevance. In the advanced course, designing an investigation is expected of students. In my Standard students’ work, the questions which would build those same skills were extra credit. I can’t tell how much of the physics students’ independence came from prior experience and how much comes from routines the teacher built. Hammond’s argument is that independence is built through opportunity, which underserved students get less of (Hammond, 2015).

Artifact 4: Classroom map and circulation path

Context and resources: Seating map · Placement Biology class · Every class period

What is happening. The red line marks the path the teacher walks continuously: a loop around the center tables and a pass up the middle aisle. The teacher checks in with every student, by name, every day. Students wave the teacher over, often more than once a period, answer honestly about how their work is going, make small talk. By doing this, the teacher can quickly spot students who are struggling and read the mood of the room. Seating charts are also flexible based on preferences or concerns that students share in conferences.

What it shows. The teacher has baked rapport-building and familiarity into the physical structure of the room (Hammond, 2015). This is especially important for the quiet, middle-of-the-pack students who are good at “playing school” and rarely hear from teachers. This is an important step in acknowledging competence.

What’s missing. There’s no written record of who actually gets contact. An interaction tally sheet on a clipboard would show it.

Artifact 5: Cell metaphor project

Context and resources: Project sheet and rubric · Placement Biology class · Cell unit

What is happening. Students invent an original metaphor for the whole cell, such as a factory. They assign each of 12 organelles and structures a matching part and justify their choices. They get teacher approval before illustrating it on a poster. Students may work in their preferred language. The rubric awards 13 points for assigning every organelle, 12 for metaphors that make sense, 12 for drawing and labeling, and 13 for logistics and looks. Four of the 50 students worked in a language other than English: three in Spanish and one in Mandarin Chinese.

What it shows. Students build the analogy from their own “funds of knowledge” instead of using a template (Hammond, 2015). The teacher-approval step builds in a mechanism for guaranteed feedback. The language choice and the art draw on linguistic capital, which includes visual art (Yosso, 2005).

What’s missing. Scientific reasoning is only responsible for less than a quarter of the grade.

Critical reflection

About 3 min

When I first encountered CRSP, my initial impression was that culturally relevant teaching fit English and Social Studies much better than a typical science course. After all, it’s difficult to connect DNA replication or oxidative phosphorylation to my students’ cultures. Rereading CRT and the Brain has changed my perspective. Hammond states clearly that culturally responsive teaching is not subject-specific or a bag of tricks; it is a way to build all students’ capacity to think (Hammond, 2015). To operationalize it is to apply those beliefs to practiced routines.

By that metric, my mentor teacher and I have operationalized aspects of CRSP, especially by building relationships with students. Every student has a one-on-one conference each quarter that begins with listening (Artifact 1), and the teacher circulates to every student, referring to them by name, every day (Artifact 4). I believe that circulation is of special importance. I have noticed that I tend to spend the most time with independent learners, because they are the ones most willing to call me over. A fixed path through the classroom means that shy students don’t have to raise and wait their hand to be seen. Furthermore, during conferences, students have told us about home situations, seating needs, and organizational struggles we would not otherwise have been aware of, and families express appreciation for being included in their child’s learning. This is aspirational and familial capital at work (Yosso, 2005).

What I have seen less of is the “demand” part of the warm demander. On the photosynthesis review assignment, the experimental-design questions were extra credit for Standard students, and no Standard students attempted them (Artifact 2). In contrast, in an advanced physics class at the same school, students design their own investigations and do science almost completely independently (Artifact 3). One lesson from CRT and the Brain is that underserved students tend to get less higher-order work (Hammond, 2015), which may actually worsen the achievement gap. The students with the fewest resources are the least likely to take on challenges (Feldman, 2024). Our students tend direct their effort according toward the minimum required points, and so do not bother with extra credit questions, especially if they are rigorous. Similarly, student conferences tend to center grades as well. The cell metaphor assignment rubric awards more points to logistics and color than to whether the metaphors make scientific sense (Artifact 5).

From these observations I have concluded that CRSP may be undermined when care supplants demand in the classroom. Hammond’s name for this is the “sentimentalist” (Hammond, 2015), and I see myself in it. My style is warm, and demanding high-quality work of all students equitably is a strength I am still developing. Our source materials offer guiding questions as we develop our teaching practices. Does this teaching practice build students’ capacity to think (Hammond, 2015)? Whose thinking gets elicited and whose competence gets acknowledged (TeachingWorks, 2026)? Do we treat what students bring to school as assets or as deficits (Yosso, 2005)?

In light of these conclusions, I will make questions worth doing required for everyone, weight rubrics toward reasoning rather than environment, translate key materials, and incorporate biology’s own non-white history, like Henrietta Lacks, into my lesson planning. My first-year goal, to design a choice-based final project scored on one shared rubric, will diversify the ways students can demonstrate mastery of the learning objectives and promote student power. My long-term goal is redesigning one unit per year around a real-world phenomenon shaped by students’ interests.

One-page handout

About 2 min

A take-away for colleagues. It stands on its own and prints on a single page.

Operationalizing Culturally Responsive & Sustaining Pedagogy

Especially in science!

Key ideas

  • Operationalizing means turning a belief into a routine that reaches every student. Culturally responsive teaching is not subject-specific or a bag of tricks. It builds every student’s capacity to think, starting from what they already know, in the context of relationships and rapport that make academic risk-taking feel safe (Hammond, 2015).
  • Care without demand is not enough. A warm demander pairs personal warmth with active demand for academic effort; warmth alone drifts toward the “sentimentalist” archetype (Hammond, 2015). When rigorous work is optional or extra credit, the students with the fewest resources are the least likely to try it (Feldman, 2024).
  • Students have assets, not deficits: aspirational, linguistic, familial and navigational capital, among others (Yosso, 2005). Ask whether each teaching practice draws on these or overlooks them.

Buzzword test. Does the teaching practice:

  1. Change how students process content and think?
  2. Ensure that every student has the best chance at being intellectually challenged?
  3. Treat what students bring as assets, not deficits to fix?

Something to try: the learning-pact conference

Turn a one-on-one check-in into a learning pact (Hammond, 2015).

  1. Listen first. Ask, “How are you?” and “What have you been doing well?”
  2. Name one strength, with evidence from the student’s work.
  3. Set one small, specific learning target: a skill, rather than a grade. Example: write a complete claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) response.
  4. Ask, “How can I help?” and name exactly what you will do.
  5. Set a check-in date a few weeks out, tied directly to that target.
  6. The student emails home with the goal and one question for the family, such as “What does my student do well at home that could help?”

Questions to carry forward

  1. Where am I warm with students but not demanding, and how specifically could I ask more of them this week?

  2. If a student never opts in to anything extra, what is the most rigorous thinking they will do in my class?

Sources: Full references in the CRSP package.
